newsitem.title: USA: Dollar jumps vs. yen as Far East currency turmoil worsens.
newsitem.headline: Dollar jumps vs. yen as Far East currency turmoil worsens.

text.p: The dollar jumped against the Japanese yen on Thursday amid concern a worsening currency crisis in Southeast Asia could damage Japan's fragile economy.

The yen slumped across the board after Indonesia announced a defacto float of its currency on Thursday, following similar actions by neighboring countries in recent weeks. Its currency, the rupiah, fell about five percent overnight, hitting a record low.
Traders feared that Japan might be forced to devalue its own currency to compete with other pacific-rim countries.
"There is definitely a spillover effect coming in from these Far Eastern devaluations," said Diane Hirschberg, a director of foreign exchange sales at Bank of Montreal in New York.

"I think the Japanese are getting concerned about that because they are major trading partners with other Far East countries and they are competing for exports to a certain extent," she said. A weaker currency makes a country's products less expensive overseas.
Traders also feared that weak export markets for Japan limits its option to raise interest rates if its economy improves, which would make yen investments more attractive.
In New York, the dollar topped 118 yen for the first time since falling more than four percent last week. It ended at 117.85 yen, up from 115.65 at Wednesday's close.
Indonesia was the last of the so called "Asian Tigers" to abandon official intervention bands. Central banks set the thresholds to buy or sell in the open market to curb their currency's movements.
Thailand kicked off the turmoil early last month by floating the baht, which had been sold heavily by investors who feared a strong currency would undermine the growth of the export-led Thai economy.

The dollar also rose against the mark, but its gains were limited by the advance of the German currency against the yen. The dollar felt additional pressure from nagging concerns that Germany might increase interest rates to strengthen the mark and contain inflation.

Bundesbank vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, in an interview on Thursday with the German newspaper Handelsblatt, said the German central bank was concerned about inflation and wanted freedom to act, which traders took as a warning it might raise short term interest rates.
Gaddum also reiterated that Bundesbank policy is not driven by foreign exchange developments, but added the bankers keep a close eye on "exaggerated" moves.

"I think he's just repeating what's been said in recent days, when the Bundesbank monthly report came out," said James Powers, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale.
"I don't think they're going to raise rates. They kind of got the dollar down to more manageable levels ... but the initial knee-jerk reaction was to sell dollars," he added.
The dollar ended at 1.8395 marks, up from 1.8345 on Wednesday. It rose to 1.5173 Swiss francs from 1.5113 but fell to Canadian $1.3905 from C$1.3929.
